article.title: JDK 27 Ships as General Availability With Post-Quantum TLS and a Universal Default G1 Garbage Collector
article.summary: JDK 27 reached general availability on September 15, 2026, with nine JEPs covering post-quantum TLS key exchange, a universal G1 default garbage collector, and compact object headers by default.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

JDK 27 reached general availability on September 15, 2026, according to [OpenJDK's project page](https://openjdk.org/projects/jdk/27/), which states that "JDK 27 reached General Availability on 15 September 2026." The release includes nine JEPs, with five of them in preview or incubator stages, according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/java27-released/). Headline changes include a universal default garbage collector, hybrid post-quantum key exchange for TLS 1.3, and compact object headers turned on by default.

The release follows a two-week delay to its first release candidate, which Oracle attributed to aligning with its Critical Patch Update cycle, as [previously reported](/article/2026-08/11-oracle-delays-jdk-27s-first-release-candidate-by-two-weeks-to-align-with-august-security-patch-cycle).

## What We Know

**G1 becomes the default garbage collector everywhere.** [JEP 523](https://openjdk.org/jeps/523) makes G1 the default across all environments, not just server-class deployments. The JEP states plainly: "The HotSpot JVM will always select G1" when no collector is specified at startup. G1 was previously made the default only for servers in JDK 9, while the Serial collector remained the default in constrained environments. According to the JEP, recent engineering work has closed that gap: "G1's maximum throughput is close to that of Serial" and "G1's maximum latencies have always been better" than Serial's, while G1's native memory usage has been brought down to levels comparable with Serial.

**Post-quantum TLS key exchange arrives via JEP 527.** [JEP 527](https://openjdk.org/jeps/527) adds hybrid key exchange algorithms for TLS 1.3 that "defend against future quantum computing attacks by combining a quantum-resistant algorithm with a traditional algorithm." Three schemes are supported: X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, and SecP384r1MLKEM1024, combining the ML-KEM post-quantum algorithm with the ECDHE curves X25519, secp256r1, and secp384r1 respectively. X25519MLKEM768 becomes the preferred scheme in the TLS handshake by default, and applications built on the `javax.net.ssl` APIs get the protection automatically without code changes. The JEP frames the motivation around a "harvest now, decrypt later" threat, in which adversaries collect encrypted traffic today to decrypt once sufficiently powerful quantum computers exist.

**Compact object headers are on by default.** [JEP 534](https://openjdk.org/jeps/534) makes compact object headers the default HotSpot object header layout, a change the JEP says will "reduce object headers from 96 bits down to 64 bits on 64-bit architectures, thereby reducing heap size, improving deployment density, and increasing data locality." The feature was introduced incrementally through JEP 450 in JDK 24 and JEP 519 in JDK 25, and the JEP cites testing from Oracle, Amazon, and SAP as validating its stability. Benchmark figures in the JEP include 22% less heap space and 8% less CPU time on SPECjbb2015, a 15% reduction in garbage-collection time with the G1 and Parallel collectors, and a parallel JSON parser benchmark running in 10% less time. The behavior can still be reverted with the `-XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders` flag.

**Structured concurrency reaches its seventh preview.** [JEP 533](https://openjdk.org/jeps/533) continues previewing an API that "treats groups of related tasks running in different threads as single units of work", aiming to simplify error handling, cancellation, and observability in concurrent code.

**The remaining JEPs round out a nine-feature release.** According to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/java27-released/), JDK 27's full JEP list also includes JEP 531 (Lazy Constants, Third Preview), JEP 532 (Primitive Types in Patterns, instanceof, and switch, Fifth Preview), JEP 536 (JFR In-Process Data Redaction), JEP 537 (Vector API, Twelfth Incubator), and JEP 538 (PEM Encodings of Cryptographic Objects, Third Preview). JEP 538 provides "an API for encoding objects that represent cryptographic keys, certificates, and certificate revocation lists into the widely-used Privacy-Enhanced Mail format", and its changes include renaming the `DEREncodable` interface to `BinaryEncodable`, according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/java27-released/).

**Related projects ship alongside the platform release.** [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/java27-released/) reports that Helidon 27 is the first release to follow a new "Tip & Tail Model", with Helidon 4.5.5 serving as the stable tail. JavaFX 27 adds a Metal rendering pipeline on macOS and enhanced text-editing controls. Oracle also shipped Jipher 20, a FIPS 140-3 cryptographic provider supporting JDK 17, 21, 25, and 27.

**Oracle has already outlined JDK 28.** Per [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/java27-released/), six JEPs are targeted for the JDK 28 release in March 2027, including two from Project Valhalla: JEP 539 (Strict Field Initialization in the JVM, Preview) and JEP 401 (Value Classes and Objects, Preview).

## What We Don't Know

The sources reviewed for this article do not specify JDK 27's long-term-support status or its official support window length. Oracle's twice-yearly release cadence alternates feature releases with periodic long-term-support versions, but neither OpenJDK's project page nor InfoQ's report of the release, as reviewed here, states where JDK 27 falls in that cycle.

## Analysis

Taken together, JDK 27's headline changes point toward the JVM narrowing its own default configuration space rather than expanding it: a single garbage collector for nearly every deployment, a single preferred post-quantum key-exchange scheme, and a single default object-header layout. For a platform historically defined by tunable defaults and opt-in flags, folding G1 and compact object headers into the baseline configuration signals that the performance data behind those features, cited in JEP 523 and JEP 534, has convinced the Java platform group that most workloads no longer benefit from the older defaults.
